extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students/critics of narrative craft
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and methods for composing and evaluating long-form literary fiction (novels), with emphasis on characterization, representation of time, point of view, and the selection and arrangement of scenes. Useful for authors planning narrative form and critics assessing technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character autonomy / realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should seem to have lives of their own beyond the limits of the book — an obvious latitude of movement in an open world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not achieved simply by description or by the author knowing the characters; the text must present them so they feel free to exist outside the narrative (Tolstoy’s people do this; Balzac’s, though exhaustively known, often feel confined to the author’s habitation). Example contrast: Tolstoy vs Balzac. Anti-pattern: characters that feel only like fixtures of the plot or whose reality depends solely on detailed backstory provided by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of space and daylight (spatial/temporal continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain continuity of space and daylight to support the book’s motive and make the world feel continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity underpins the sense that events and characters inhabit a coherent world; it is 'so necessary to the motive of the book' and is demonstrated in War and Peace. Discontinuous or fragmentary treatment of space/time can weaken the novel’s sense of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the passage of time (the form of time)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of time — not just the content ordered in time — must be represented; the lines and masses of the book should show the movement of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely listing stages or announcing 'years have fled' is insufficient. The build of the whole book must make the passage perceptible: show time in faces, gestures, thought texture, and by structural shaping (the wheel, the curve of generations). Example: War and Peace makes time present through continuous development and shifts in temperament and status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveying the sweep of a life-cycle in a limited span
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the action covers a relatively short period (e.g., fifteen years), the narrative must make the whole sweep or 'large circumference' of life apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the revolution of life (rise and fall of a generation) feel large even when only a segment is shown — e.g., show newcomers, changing expectations, and the contrast between youth’s promise and middle-age settlement to reveal the curve of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraying age and consistent development
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the noiseless, believable progression of age: characters must grow older while retaining essential sameness/consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render changes so that mutability never hides continuity. Example: mastery at showing a young person becoming middle-aged with continuity of personality and believable change (Tolstoy). Anti-pattern: abrupt or unmotivated personality shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and moral/structural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel needs an overall design: the chapters and scenes should collocate to announce a reason for their grouping; the picture should have a moral or form that justifies the selection of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral or design is in the form; without design, scattered scenes fail to make a coherent picture. Anti-pattern: vacillation of purpose where chapters refuse to adapt to a single effect, producing uncertainty and confusion of lines (as Tolstoy sometimes does in the essay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain subjectal focus and consistency of intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the subject and the author's purpose fixed throughout composition so the material accumulates toward a single effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ranges around the material without deciding the end to which it is amassed. If the novelist’s intention shifts, valuable material is wasted or diminishes the central picture. Example contrast: Flaubert's Bovary — subject remained fixed during years of revision; Tolstoy sometimes wanders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and economical use of facts (facts must be used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are raw material but have no validity until chosen and used to create an image; the novelist must select information to make the intended effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel is not merely a row of facts; the art lies in the method of choosing path and placing statements so the book looks true without external attestation. Anti-pattern: dumping unselected facts or treating the novel as a mere information report (contrast with Defoe-like attestation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic vs panoramic presentation (choice of viewpoint scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide when to present particular scenes (scenic, immediate hours) and when to take a panoramic or summarizing view of a stretch of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are fundamental method distinctions. A critic/reader watches how alternation is managed: scene should prepare and illuminate the chronicle, and summaries should set up scenes. Failure to manage alternation can leave scenes unprepared or ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view selection and shifts (authorial vs character perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether to present events from the author’s vantage (broad knowledge, omniscient narration) or through a character’s consciousness (subjective viewpoint), and manage shifts consciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts change what the reader knows and how events are coloured (Flaubert moves between authorial summary and Emma’s interior view). Use authorial intervention when broader knowledge is required; use character viewpoint to dramatize mood and perception. Keep shifts intelligible and motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial presence and impersonality (voice management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control the author's visible judgement: an 'impersonal' effect is achieved by dramatizing opinions rather than openly stating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even 'impersonal' writers reveal opinion by selection and dramatization. The craft is to express judgement tactfully through scene and characterization rather than explicit authorial commentary; but the novelist must realize that choices reveal values and cannot be neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (mood/inner impression) versus dramatic (objective scene) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to render an episode pictorially (bathed in a character’s mood, inner impression) or dramatically (detached presentation of actions and dialogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictorial treatment immerses the reader in subjective climate (e.g., Emma at the ball); dramatic treatment places the reader before visible facts that could be staged (e.g., the cattle-show). Mixing is allowed, but the choice affects how the episode functions; some effects require one method over the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character treatment across contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must remain 'true to themselves' across different settings (peace and war, private and public), ensuring continuity of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy’s strength is that his characters remain the people we know whether in peace or war. Inconsistent handling (characters behaving out of nature for convenience) weakens believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and placement of scenes (dramatic economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place and prepare occasions so they occur where 'everything is ready for it' and illuminate the subject; avoid scenes that do 'nothing in particular.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scene that lacks preparation or fails to forward the book’s purpose is a weakness. The author must arrange chronicle and scene so the occasion fulfils its illuminating or advancing role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate intervention by the author (use of retrospective/background and interiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use authorial intervention (background, retrospective facts, interior thought) when necessary to supply knowledge the immediate scene cannot provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes the reader must be told past circumstances or interior trains of thought to understand an incident; the author should intervene judiciously to supply that superior knowledge without breaking the chosen manner unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing representative vs particular roles of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character functions as a representative symbol (e.g., the spirit of youth), preserve that representative role rather than reducing them to a mere personal romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narrowing a character who initially stands for a larger theme by letting them be consumed by a specific plotline that strips them of their representative value (example: Natasha becoming merely the heroine of a romance weakens her earlier representative role).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding superficial devices for suggesting time
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suggest elapsed time by superficial devices (e.g., a row of stars or an unsupported announcement that 'years have fled'); instead make lapse of time perceptible through structure and character change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers perceive time through accumulation of development, changes in thought, gesture, and consistent structural shaping. Anti-pattern: relying on shorthand markers to stand in for real narrative representation of time.
